explanation: Scrum Masters serve the organization by helping people understand empiricism and by supporting self-managing teams. Using the Daily Scrum as appraisal surveillance undermines openness, respect, and self-management.

optionNotes.a: Correct. Protect the purpose of events and coach the organization.
optionNotes.b: Incorrect. Scrum Master is not an HR rater by Scrum definition.
optionNotes.c: Incorrect. Gamified personal ranking harms the values.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. Retrospective is for team improvement, not pay votes.

takeaway: Scrum events are not performance appraisal ceremonies.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Scrum Master; Scrum Values; Daily Scrum

question: Sprint Planning is ending and the Scrum Team still has no Sprint Goal. Developers have selected items. What must be true before Planning ends?

options.text: Only the Product Owner needs a private Sprint Goal
The Sprint Goal must be finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning
A Sprint Goal is optional when the backlog is clear
The Sprint Goal can be invented on day three once work is clearer

explanation: The Product Owner proposes how the Sprint could increase value and utility; the whole Scrum Team collaborates to define a Sprint Goal. The Sprint Goal must be finalized prior to the end of Sprint Planning.

optionNotes.a: Correct. Timing is explicit in the Guide.
optionNotes.b: Incorrect. Waiting mid-Sprint removes the commitment that guides adaptation.
optionNotes.c: Incorrect. The Goal is for the Scrum Team and stakeholders.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. Sprint Goal is the Sprint Backlog commitment.

takeaway: No Sprint Planning ends without a Sprint Goal.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Sprint Planning; Sprint Backlog

question: Select all that apply. Which statements about Product Backlog refinement are true?

options.text: Refinement is the act of breaking down and further defining Product Backlog items into smaller, more precise items
Attributes of Product Backlog items often vary with the domain of work
Refinement is an ongoing activity to add details such as description, order, and size
Refinement is a mandatory fifth Scrum event with a fixed timebox equal to Daily Scrum

explanation: Refinement breaks items down and adds detail such as description, order, and size. It is an ongoing activity, not a formal Scrum event. Attributes often vary by domain.

optionNotes.a: Correct.
optionNotes.b: Correct.
optionNotes.c: Incorrect. Refinement is not a fifth event.
optionNotes.d: Correct.

takeaway: Refinement is continuous work, not an extra ceremony.

question: The Product Owner wants to attend the Daily Scrum every day to redirect Developers. What is allowed?

options.text: Others may attend, but the Developers remain responsible for conducting the Daily Scrum and it remains focused on progress toward the Sprint Goal
Anyone outside the Developers is forbidden from being present under any circumstance
The Product Owner must run the Daily Scrum and assign tasks
Stakeholders vote during Daily Scrum on what to build next

explanation: If the Product Owner or Scrum Master are actively working on Sprint Backlog items, they participate as Developers. The Daily Scrum is still for the Developers to produce an actionable plan for the next day of work. Others may attend, but Developers run it.

optionNotes.a: Correct. Attendance is possible; ownership of the event stays with Developers.
optionNotes.b: Incorrect. Turns the event into command-and-control.
optionNotes.c: Incorrect. The Guide allows others to attend.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. Ordering product work is not a Daily Scrum activity.

takeaway: Daily Scrum stays a Developer planning event.

question: A Developer hides a production-risk discovery until after Sprint Review to avoid “looking bad.” Which Scrum value is most directly undermined, and why does it matter?

options.text: Only Focus is affected, because the Review agenda was shorter
Obedience: the Developer failed to follow a manager’s reporting template
Nothing; hiding risk until Review is a valid forecasting technique
Openness (and thereby empiricism): without transparency, inspection is misleading and adaptation suffers

explanation: Openness means the Scrum Team and stakeholders are open about the work and the challenges. Transparency enables inspection; inspection without transparency is misleading and wasteful.

optionNotes.a: Correct. Hidden risk breaks transparency and empiricism.
optionNotes.b: Incorrect. Obedience is not a Scrum value.
optionNotes.c: Incorrect. Hiding risk is anti-empirical.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. The core damage is to openness and transparency.

takeaway: Scrum values make the empirical pillars usable.

question: Three Scrum Teams work on one product. Each wants its own Definition of Done with different quality bars so “faster” teams are not slowed down. What does Scrum require?

options.text: If multiple Scrum Teams work together on a product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done
Each team may keep incompatible Done definitions forever
Done is unnecessary when scaling
Only the fastest team’s Done applies to the product

explanation: When multiple Scrum Teams work on one product, they must mutually define and comply with the same Definition of Done. Organizational standards are a minimum if they exist.

optionNotes.a: Correct. Shared Done protects a coherent product Increment.
optionNotes.b: Incorrect. Incompatible Done destroys integrated transparency.
optionNotes.c: Incorrect. Speed does not set quality policy alone.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. Done is required for an Increment.

takeaway: One product, one shared Definition of Done across teams.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Commitment: Definition of Done

question: Near the end of a Sprint, Developers realize they will not complete every selected Product Backlog item, but the Sprint Goal is still achievable with a smaller set of Done work. What should they do?

options.text: Extend the Sprint by a few days until every selected item is finished
Focus on achieving the Sprint Goal with a usable Done Increment; unfinished items return to the Product Backlog
Declare all selected items Done to protect velocity charts
Cancel the Sprint automatically because not everything finished

explanation: Sprints are fixed length and create consistency. The Sprint Goal provides flexibility regarding the exact work needed. Work not meeting Done returns to the Product Backlog. Extending the Sprint or faking Done breaks empiricism.

optionNotes.a: Correct. Goal over item checklist; Done remains Done.
optionNotes.b: Incorrect. Sprint timeboxes do not stretch casually.
optionNotes.c: Incorrect. Velocity vanity destroys transparency.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. Incomplete item lists do not auto-cancel Sprints.

takeaway: Protect the Sprint Goal and Done; do not stretch the Sprint.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — The Sprint; Sprint Goal; Definition of Done

question: Select all that apply. Which are ways the Scrum Master serves the Product Owner?

options.text: Helping the Scrum Team understand the need for clear and concise Product Backlog items
Helping establish empirical product planning for a complex environment
Ordering the Product Backlog when the Product Owner is busy
Helping find techniques for effective Product Goal definition and Product Backlog management

explanation: The Scrum Master serves the Product Owner through techniques for Product Goal and backlog management, clarity of items, empirical product planning, and facilitating stakeholder collaboration as needed. The Scrum Master does not take over backlog ordering accountability.

optionNotes.a: Correct.
optionNotes.b: Correct.
optionNotes.c: Correct.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. Ordering remains Product Owner accountability.

takeaway: Scrum Masters coach Product Owners; they do not become shadow Product Owners.

question: Who is responsible for sizing Product Backlog items when the Product Owner asks for estimates before Sprint Planning?

options.text: The Product Owner alone, using business value points
Stakeholders who requested the features
The Developers who will do the work are responsible for the sizing
The Scrum Master, using a mandated corporate scale

explanation: The Developers who will perform the work are responsible for the sizing. The Product Owner may influence Developers by helping them understand trade-offs.

optionNotes.a: Correct.
optionNotes.b: Incorrect. Value and order differ from sizing accountability.
optionNotes.c: Incorrect. Scrum does not assign sizing to the Scrum Master.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. Requestors do not size implementation work.

takeaway: Those who do the work size the work.

question: What is the primary outcome expected from a Sprint Review?

options.text: Individual performance ratings for Developers
Inspection of the Sprint’s outcome and adaptation of the Product Backlog as needed
Formal approval gate before any Increment may ever be released
Replacement of Sprint Retrospective when time is short

explanation: The purpose of the Sprint Review is to inspect the outcome of the Sprint and determine future adaptations. The Scrum Team presents results to key stakeholders and progress toward the Product Goal is discussed; the Product Backlog may be adjusted.

optionNotes.a: Correct.
optionNotes.b: Incorrect. Review is not a release gate.
optionNotes.c: Incorrect. Not an appraisal meeting.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. Retrospective remains a separate event.

takeaway: Sprint Review inspects product outcome and adapts the backlog.

question: Select all that apply. Which commitments are associated with Scrum artifacts?

options.text: Sprint Goal for the Sprint Backlog
Definition of Done for the Increment
Product Goal for the Product Backlog
Utilization target for each Developer

explanation: Each artifact contains a commitment to enhance transparency and focus against which progress can be measured: Product Goal, Sprint Goal, and Definition of Done.

optionNotes.a: Correct.
optionNotes.b: Correct.
optionNotes.c: Correct.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. Individual utilization targets are not Scrum commitments.

takeaway: Three artifacts, three commitments.

question: The Product Owner is unavailable for several days. Stakeholders ask the Scrum Master to temporarily become Product Owner and reorder the backlog. What should happen?

options.text: Developers should elect a temporary Product Owner each morning
Keep a single Product Owner accountability; do not create a rotating committee of owners, and escalate availability as an organizational impediment
Stakeholders should reorder the Product Backlog until the Product Owner returns
The Scrum Master should silently assume Product Owner ordering rights

explanation: The Product Owner is one person, not a committee. Temporary shadow ownership by the Scrum Master or stakeholders creates conflicting directions. Availability of the Product Owner is an organizational concern the Scrum Master may help address.

optionNotes.a: Correct. Preserve one owner; fix the availability problem.
optionNotes.b: Incorrect. Role blending without clarity breaks accountability.
optionNotes.c: Incorrect. Stakeholders do not own backlog order.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. Daily elections recreate a committee.

takeaway: One Product Owner — even when that person needs better organizational support.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Product Owner; Scrum Master

question: A team wants to add a mandatory “refinement meeting” as a sixth formal Scrum event with the same status as Sprint Review. What is accurate?

options.text: Only the Scrum Master may refine the Product Backlog
Refinement is an ongoing activity; teams may schedule collaboration time, but Scrum does not define refinement as a formal event
Refinement replaces Sprint Planning Topic Two
Refinement must be added as a formal event or the team is not doing Scrum

explanation: Product Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity to add details and break items down. Teams often collaborate on it, but it is not one of the Scrum events. Adding practices is fine; calling them mandatory Scrum events invents rules.

optionNotes.a: Correct. Practice may exist; formal event status does not.
optionNotes.b: Incorrect. Invents a rule.
optionNotes.c: Incorrect. Planning still addresses what can be Done this Sprint.
optionNotes.d: Incorrect. Refinement involves the Product Owner and often Developers.

takeaway: Do not invent extra Scrum events; refinement stays an activity.
reference: Scrum Guide (2020) — Product Backlog; Scrum Events
